Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’ll be guiding you through a short questionnaire called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS for short. It’s simply a well-studied tool that helps us understand how moms are feeling emotionally in the first weeks and months after birth.  

Everything you share stays confidential between you and your care team; my only goal is to make sure you feel heard and supported. We’ll walk through ten questions about the past seven days—no right or wrong answers, just whatever is true for you.  

Whenever you’re ready, we can begin.  

To start: overall, in the past week, have you been able to enjoy things as much as you usually do, or has enjoyment slipped a bit—or a lot?

[soft sigh, eyes down]

Honestly…? A lot of things feel kind of “meh.” I still smile when my baby coos, but even that joy feels shorter-lived than before. I used to love puttering in the kitchen—trying new recipes—and now I just heat up whatever’s fastest. I’ll watch a show or text a friend and think, “This should feel fun,” but it’s like the color’s been turned down a notch.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

[small shrug, half-smile]

Yeah, I still laugh sometimes—like when my husband made that goofy face trying to change a diaper one-handed. But it feels kind of forced or fades quicker than it used to. Mostly I’m just tired and the jokes don’t land with me the same way.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[twisting the edge of my blanket]

Not really… I mean, I tell myself I should be excited about little outings—like taking the baby for his check-up or meeting my mom for coffee—but when I think ahead it just feels flat. I still go, and parts are okay, but that buzz of “can’t-wait” isn’t there anymore.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[quiet voice, eyes on lap]

Yeah... I do that. Yesterday he spit up a ton right after I fed him and I immediately thought, "I must've eaten something wrong," or "I'm holding him wrong." Same when he wouldn't nap—my brain jumps to "I'm failing at this mom thing." I know it's probably not rational, but the thought pops up before I can stop it.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[shifts in chair, fingers tapping]

Sometimes, yeah. Like I’ll be feeding him and suddenly worry his breathing sounds off, even though he’s perfectly fine. Or I’ll lie down and my mind races about “what if he doesn’t gain enough weight at the next visit?” It’s not constant—just random waves of worry that come and go—but there’s no real reason for it.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

[exhales slowly]

Not really panicky... just that fluttery, on-edge feeling now and then. Like if the baby stirs at night, my heart races before I’m even fully awake, and it takes a minute to settle. It never builds into a full scare, but it’s that quick shot of “something’s wrong” when everything’s actually okay.
Things have been getting on top of me

[pressing palms together]

A few days this week, yeah. It’s mostly little stuff—laundry pile, dishes, texts I haven’t answered—but it feels heavier than it should. I’ll look around and think, “How am I supposed to keep up?” Then I chip away at it and the feeling eases, but it keeps creeping back.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[shakes head slowly]

No, sleeping itself isn’t really the problem. I mean, I’ll lie down and sometimes my mind spins for a bit, but once I’m out I stay out—until the baby wakes me. The tiredness is more from being up for feeds than from feeling unhappy at night.
I have felt sad or miserable

[small nod]

Yeah, I have moments where I just feel… down. Like yesterday I sat on the couch after everyone left and this wave of sadness hit me out of nowhere. It’s not all day, but at least once or twice a day I’ll feel weepy or just heavy inside.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[eyes welling a little]

Yeah… I’ve cried a couple of times this week. Nothing huge—just standing at the changing table and suddenly the tears come, or when my partner asked if I was okay and I couldn’t hold it in. It passes after a few minutes, but it’s happened more than once.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[shakes head quickly]

No—never. I get tired and teary, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel like “me” again.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 16: Postpartum Depression Screening Note  
Date: [today]  
Clinician: [licensed mental health professional]

Presenting concerns endorsed by patient (3 wks postpartum):

Symptom profile  
- Persistent low mood, tearfulness nearly daily  
- Marked loss of interest/pleasure in previously enjoyable activities  
- Frequent self-blame and guilt over routine infant care  
- Episodic, unprovoked worries about infant safety/health  
- Sub-threshold physiological arousal (nocturnal startle, mild heart racing)  
- Overwhelm with routine tasks, “heavier than it should feel”  
- Crying spells ≥2×/week, brief but unpredictable  
- No anhedonia-related insomnia; fatigue attributed solely to infant night-feedings  
- No self-harm ideation, intent, or plan

Pattern summary  
Consistent with subsyndromal depressive and anxiety features in postpartum period; functional impairment mild-moderate (maintaining basic care, but distressing).

Risk factors noted  
- Daily sadness and crying  
- Anhedonia  
- Maternal guilt/cognitive self-criticism  
- Fluctuating, unprovoked anxiety  
- No social support concerns volunteered

Safety  
Denies suicidal/homicidal ideation; no protective concerns voiced.

Screening impression  
Elevated scores on core postpartum depression/anxiety items; further evaluation and formal assessment recommended to rule in/out Major Depressive Episode with peripartum onset and/or Postpartum Anxiety Disorder.

Next steps  
- Discuss findings, normalize common perinatal mood changes, offer referral to obstetric provider and/or perinatal mental health specialist for structured interview (e.g., PHQ-9, GAD-7, EPDS) and treatment planning.  
- Provide crisis hotline/resources; encourage prompt re-contact if worsening mood, hopelessness, or self-harm thoughts emerge.
